content.title: About
content.content: A burrito bowl is a Mexican‑inspired dish served in a bowl with rice, beans, vegetables, cheese, and a choice of meat (beef or pork). It is typically topped with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream, making it easy to eat without a tortilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bowl version emerged as a lighter alternative to the traditional wrapped burrito.
Brown rice is often used in authentic recipes for added nutrients.
Meat can be grilled, smoked with chipotle, or marinated in lime and spices.
The dish is popular across the United States and Canada, especially in fast‑casual chains.
Beef offers a leaner profile, while pork provides a richer, more robust flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and pork supply complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Beans and vegetables add dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and beans are rich in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Guacamole and a modest amount of cheese contribute monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and fiber helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: If the sauce contains wheat flour or soy sauce, it may trigger reactions in gluten‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and marinades can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Cheese fat
items.content: Hard cheese adds saturated fat, which should be limited by those monitoring cholesterol.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The bowl can be calorie‑rich due to rice, meat, beans, and sauces; balance it within your daily intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burrito bowl in a deep dish. Toss all ingredients together, add sauce to taste, and enjoy with a fork or spoon. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, or crunchy tortilla chips if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If not eaten immediately, store the bowl in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep sauces and guacamole separate to prevent soggy rice and beans. Reheat rice and meat before serving.

chicken-or-turkey-shish-kabob-with-veget.title: Chicken or Turkey Shish Kabob with Vegetables (No Potatoes)

content.title: About
content.content: A shish kabob made from chicken or turkey breast pieces threaded with vegetables such as bell pepper, onion, zucchini and cherry tomatoes, grilled over open flame or on a grill pan. The dish is high in protein, vitamins and minerals while being free of potatoes, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are among the most widely consumed meats worldwide due to their affordability and availability.
Marinating the meat in lemon juice, olive oil and spices tenderizes it and adds aromatic flavor.
The vegetables used are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.
Grilling meat on an open fire is an ancient tradition found in many cultures.
Excluding potatoes lowers the glycemic index of the meal, which can help blood‑sugar control.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared properly
items.content: Using lean breast meat and moderate oil keeps the dish relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc and phosphorus in the meat contribute to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell peppers, tomatoes and zucchini provide vitamin C and carotenoids that boost immunity.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to poultry or to certain spices used in the marinade.

items.title: Improper thawing
items.content: Thawing meat at room temperature can promote bacterial growth; always thaw in the refrigerator.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Excessive grilling can create carcinogenic compounds; monitor cooking time carefully.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: High salt levels in the marinade may increase blood pressure risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the kabobs hot, straight from the grill. They can be enjoyed as a main dish or paired with a light green salad. Eat the vegetables together with the meat for added moisture and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked kabobs keep in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days in an airtight container. Do not freeze the cooked product, as texture will deteriorate. Raw meat and vegetables should be stored separately and used within 24 hours.

collards-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Collards, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Collard greens are dark‑green leafy vegetables belonging to the Brassicaceae family. The frozen, cooked without added fat version retains most of its nutrients, a mildly bitter flavor, and a firm texture after thawing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards are often called “winter kale” because they store well at low temperatures.
Unlike spinach, collard leaves are thicker, making them ideal for freezing.
In the United States collards are a staple of Southern cuisine, frequently cooked with ham or bacon.
Collard leaves are rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification pathways.
Frozen collards are usually blanched before freezing to preserve their bright color and nutrients.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Collards provide over 800% of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene in collards converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Minerals: calcium, iron, magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for bone strength, blood formation, and nerve function.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collards contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: High amounts of glucosinolates may affect thyroid function if iodine intake is low.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thawed collards can be added to soups, stews, vegetable mixes, pasta dishes, or used as a base for salads. They also taste great sautéed quickly with a drizzle of olive oil and your favorite spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen collards in an airtight bag at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and store in the refrigerator in a sealed container.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, sweet quick‑bread made with flour, eggs, milk, sugar and a leavening agent. This version incorporates wheat bran (2500 g), boosting dietary fiber and nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bran is the outer layer of the wheat kernel and is rich in fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals.
Adding bran to the batter makes muffins denser and gives them a nutty flavor.
Muffins are often packaged as single servings, making them a popular snack at work and school.
Traditionally muffins are baked in metal or silicone cups, but paper liners are also common.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Bran provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Bran contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Bran supplies magnesium, iron and zinc.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The fiber in bran helps moderate blood‑sugar spikes compared with regular sweet baked goods.

items.title: May aid weight control
items.content: Fiber promotes satiety, which can help reduce overall calorie intake.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Typical muffin recipes contain a lot of sugar; moderation is advised.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite the added bran, muffins remain calorie‑dense due to fats and sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, split and topped with cottage cheese, yogurt or nut butter. They are convenient to pack in a lunchbox.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags – they keep well for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pear (Pyrus communis) is a sweet, juicy fruit with a rounded base and tapered neck, native to Europe and western Asia. It has thin skin in green, yellow, red, or brown shades and soft, slightly gritty flesh. Pears are eaten fresh and used in desserts, salads, baking, and preserves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pears are related to apples and roses.
Unlike many fruits, European pears ripen best off the tree and are usually picked while still firm.
Popular varieties include Bartlett, Anjou, Bosc, and Comice, and Asian pears are round and crisp.
A pear is ripe when the area near the stem yields slightly to gentle pressure.
Pears have been cultivated for thousands of years.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Pears are a good source of fiber, including pectin, especially with the skin.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: These vitamins support the immune system and blood clotting.

items.title: Provides potassium and copper
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure and metabolism.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Pears contain plant compounds with antioxidant properties, mainly in the skin.

items.title: Hydrating
items.content: Pears are juicy and refreshing.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Pears contain fructose and sorbitol, which may cause gas, bloating, or loose stools in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people, especially those allergic to birch pollen, may experience itching or tingling in the mouth.

items.title: Natural sugars
items.content: Pears contain natural sugars, and juice provides less fiber than the whole fruit.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Wash pears thoroughly before eating, especially if eating the skin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pears can be eaten fresh with the skin on, sliced into salads, paired with cheese and nuts, baked, poached, or cooked into compotes, jams, and desserts. Eating the whole fruit provides the most fiber. Sprinkle cut pears with lemon juice to slow browning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep firm pears at room temperature until they ripen, then store ripe pears in the refrigerator for three to five days. Keep them away from other produce, because ripe pears release ethylene gas. Cut pears can be stored in an airtight container for a day or two.

rice-brown-cooked-made-with-margarine.title: Rice, brown, cooked, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran and germ. When cooked with a small amount of margarine it gains a subtle buttery flavor and a tender texture while staying nutrient‑dense.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Margarine used in cooking is often fortified with vitamins A and D.
In the 1970s brown rice became popular in the United States as a “health” alternative.
When stored properly, whole grains keep a nutty aroma for up to six months.
In Japan brown rice is frequently served with soy sauce and seaweed.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for bone health, muscle function, and nerve signaling.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3, and B6 play key roles in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Beneficial fats from margarine
items.content: Fortified margarine can add vitamin D and omega‑6 fatty acids, which support skin and immune health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice raises blood glucose more slowly than white rice, making it suitable for glycemic control.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can bind minerals and reduce their absorption; soaking the rice before cooking can mitigate this.

items.title: Caloric contribution of margarine
items.content: Adding margarine increases the dish’s calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may react to components of certain margarines.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Choose trans‑fat‑free margarine to avoid adverse cardiovascular effects.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side to vegetables, fish, or poultry. It works well in salads, soups, and casseroles. Add fresh herbs, lemon juice, or soy sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to steaming temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed potatoes, Puerto Rican style is a traditional dish from Puerto Rico that consists of potatoes slowly simmered in a fragrant sauce made from tomatoes, sweet peppers, onions, garlic, olive oil, and characteristic Puerto Rican spices such as adobo and cumin. It is often served as a side dish with meat, fish, or beans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated during the colonial era when Spanish and African culinary traditions blended with local ingredients.
In Puerto Rico the potatoes are traditionally cooked in clay pots (guiseros), which impart a unique earthy flavor.
Red potatoes are commonly used because they hold their shape during long stewing.
The sauce is often enriched with a “pasta” – a pre‑cooked blend of tomatoes, peppers, and spices.
Stewed potatoes are frequently accompanied by “mojo” – a sauce of avocado, lime, and olive oil.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Potatoes provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes and sweet peppers add vitamin C, which helps boost the immune system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Only a modest amount of olive oil is used, keeping the dish relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and polyphenols from the spices have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Heart‑friendly fats
items.content: Olive oil contributes monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to cumin, adobo, or other spices used in the recipe.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is made with canned tomato paste or broth, the sodium level can be high.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stewed potatoes hot as a side with grilled meat, fish, chicken, or beans. They also work well in tacos, burritos, or as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.
